name: Bumetanide

card.summary: A potent prescription loop diuretic that appears in gray-market "water pill" talk; no study has tested it for facial puffiness.
card.note: Carries a boxed warning about profound fluid and electrolyte loss; banned in sport by WADA.

quick.overview:
Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that makes the kidneys excrete more salt and water. It is prescribed for swelling caused by heart, liver or kidney disease.

It has been added to this wiki because it is discussed as a gray-market "water pill" for rapid water-weight loss. No published study has examined it for facial depuffing or any appearance goal.
quick.mechanism: It blocks the NKCC2 sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, so less sodium and water are reabsorbed and urine output rises. Effects begin within about an hour and last around six hours.[1][2]
quick.risks: The US label carries a boxed warning that excessive amounts can cause profound water and electrolyte depletion and requires medical supervision. Reported effects include cramps, dizziness, low blood pressure, low potassium and, rarely, hearing loss and serious skin reactions. It is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[3][1]

lead: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic, a prescription medicine that increases the amount of sodium and water the kidneys excrete. It is sold as Bumex, Burinex and, in a nasal-spray form, Enbumyst, among other names, and is used to treat edema (fluid retention) associated with heart failure, liver disease and kidney disease.[1][3]

On a milligram basis it is described as roughly 40 times more potent than furosemide, with more complete and predictable oral absorption.[1][2] It is listed on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List.[1]

In appearance-focused communities it is mentioned as a stronger water pill for temporarily reducing water retention. No published clinical study has tested bumetanide for cosmetic depuffing. Its US label states that excessive amounts can produce profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion and that careful medical supervision is required.[3]

paras: Bumetanide is approved in the United States for edema associated with congestive heart failure and hepatic and renal disease, including nephrotic syndrome.[3] Wikipedia notes that it may work when other diuretics do not, and that it is not a preferred treatment for high blood pressure.[1]
It can be taken by mouth or given by injection into a vein or muscle; the label notes a nearly equal response after oral and parenteral administration.[3]

The label lists muscle cramps, dizziness, low blood pressure, headache, nausea and, in people with liver disease, encephalopathy as the most frequent reactions, reported in about 4% of treated patients. Serious skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis have been reported.[3]

Excessive use can lead to dehydration, reduced blood volume, circulatory collapse and a risk of clots, particularly in older people, and low potassium can occur.[3] Wikipedia also lists hearing loss (ototoxicity) and low platelet counts among serious risks and recommends regular blood tests.[1]

Bumetanide inhibits the NKCC2 cotransporter in the loop of Henle, reducing reabsorption of sodium, chloride and potassium and increasing water loss.[2][1] In the brain it also blocks the related NKCC1 transporter, which is the basis of research interest outside kidney disease.[1][4]
Oral absorption is high (about 80% or more), the drug is heavily protein-bound and metabolised in the liver, and the elimination half-life is short, around 0.8 hours in adults.[1][2]

Bumetanide was patented in 1968 and entered medical use in 1972; Grokipedia attributes its synthesis to a screening programme at Leo Pharmaceutical Products in Denmark.[1][2] The US FDA approved the oral tablets in 1983 and generics followed in the 1990s.[2] In September 2025 the FDA approved a nasal-spray formulation for outpatient edema, according to Grokipedia.[2]

The drug is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and is banned under World Anti-Doping Agency rules. In 2008 four NFL players were suspended for its use, and it was found as an undisclosed ingredient in the StarCaps weight-loss supplement, which was withdrawn after an FDA investigation.[1]

Bumetanide is discussed in depuffing and water-weight contexts as a potent gray-market diuretic. No cosmetic outcome studies exist, and the sources reviewed for this article contain no detailed community threads about it.

Laboratory work found that NKCC1 contributes to excitatory GABA signalling and seizures in the immature brain, and a rodent study reported that maternal bumetanide treatment restored normal neuronal activity in offspring in autism models.[4][5] Wikipedia notes interest in bumetanide as a possible antiepileptic and in autism, with some trials reporting positive effects.[1]

No studies found on bumetanide for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Registered clinical trials examine it for other conditions, including autism in children (a 60-participant phase 3 trial) and advanced chronic kidney disease in combination with chlortalidone (a phase 2 trial with 34 participants).[6][7]
